In this project, EV charging stations are strategically placed at different nodes within the feeder. Two types of chargers are considered based on hardware characterization tests performed for this study: 350-kW and 25-kW units. In addition to the charging infrastructure, the model incorporates a PV plant and an energy storage system to represent DER. The energy storage system plays a key role in enhancing grid resilience and mitigating fluctuations in power supply and demand. Control algorithms governing these resources are implemented within the RSCAD environment in RTDS hardware-in-the-loop platform. Converters are modeled as voltage sources equipped with active and reactive power controllers, with power set points supplied by SCM. The power system simulation is executed with a time step of 60 s, enabling high-fidelity, real-time emulation of dynamic interactions between the DER, EV charging infrastructure, and grid. 𝜇𝜇 Node 650 in Figure 18 is modeled as the slack bus, with a 4.16-kV voltage and a short circuit ratio (SCR) of 10, representing a relatively strong grid. SCR is a widely used metric for assessing grid strength, defined as the ratio of short-circuit power to the rated power of the connected devices. A higher SCR indicates a stiff, reliable grid with low sensitivity to disturbances and voltage fluctuations, while grids with SCR values below 3 are typically classified as weak. Figure 18. Each arrival triggers the proximity function and sends the vehicle’s SOC to the SCM. A mapping file containing all EVSE IDs and their power ratings is accessible to both the SCM and the facility operator. Using this information, the SCM assigns the EV to a charger and communicates the EVSE ID to the operator. In making this assignment, the SCM considers multiple factors, including PV generation, energy storage system SOC, utility prices, and current or forecasted load/generation. Once the EVSE ID is received by a CHIL device, the charging process begins. The CHIL device replicates the EV’s power consumption according to its transfer function. During charging, the CHIL sends OCPP messages (e.g., MeterValues for consumed power and SOC) to the OCPP server hosted in Node-RED. Simultaneously, it communicates with the RTDS, providing signals for use within the RSCAD simulation model. The RSCAD model also simulates other sources and loads in parallel and exchanges data with the SCM in real time. The charging process ends in either of two cases: 1. The SOC reaches 80%. 2. The SCM sends a zero-power set point command to a charger, which the CHIL interprets as an instruction to terminate the session.
